pages.c02-p04: Explain what Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) is and how to prevent it

pages.c02-p07: Know the law on health and safety at work and eight things employers must do to keep ICT users safe

q.q: Which three things must we keep safe when using ICT?
o: The network, the internet and our email
The printers, the paper and the ink
The equipment, our data and ourselves
Our passwords, our files and our phones
q.why: When using computers we keep the equipment, our data and ourselves safe.

q.q: What is a hazard?
o: A rule that tells you how to use a computer safely
A punishment for breaking the computer room rules
Any source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects
Damage that has already been done to equipment
q.why: A hazard is a danger or risk: any source of potential damage, harm or adverse health effects.

q.q: You notice a frayed cable behind a computer. What should you do?
o: Report it to the teacher straight away
Wrap it in sticky tape to cover the wires
Unplug it and carry on using the computer
Move the cable so nobody else can see it
q.why: Damaged equipment can cause an electric shock: don't touch it, report it to the teacher straight away.

q.q: Which is the best way to stop people tripping over cables?
o: Tidy them away under desks or in cable covers
Tape a warning sign to the wall
Put bags on top of them so they don't move
Leave them in the walkway where they can be seen
q.why: Trailing cables should be tidied away under desks or in cable covers.

q.q: What could happen if too many devices are plugged into one socket?
o: Repetitive Strain Injury
Eye strain and headaches
A virus spreading to the network
Overheating and fire
q.why: Overloaded plug sockets can overheat and cause a fire.

q.q: Why is food and drink banned near computers?
o: Spills can cause electric shocks or damage keyboards
Eating causes eye strain at the screen
Crumbs slow down the school network
Drinks make the room too hot for computers
q.why: Spills can cause electric shocks or damage keyboards, so there is no food or drink in the ICT room.

q.q: Which hazard is best dealt with by putting bags under desks?
o: Glare on the screen
Electric shocks from damaged plugs
People tripping over things in walkways
Overheating computers
q.why: Bags and coats on the floor are a trip hazard; put bags under desks and keep walkways clear.

q.q: The ICT room is very hot and stuffy. What problem could this cause?
o: RSI in the wrists and fingers from typing
Headaches, tiredness and computers overheating
People tripping over trailing cables
Viruses spreading and data being lost
q.why: A room that is too hot with poor air flow causes headaches, tiredness and overheating computers.

q.q: Which is a sensible way to deal with a room that is too hot?
o: Open windows, use fans and keep vents clear
Turn the brightness of all screens up
Plug more fans into one socket
Cover the computer vents to keep heat in
q.why: Open windows, use air conditioning or fans and keep vents clear.

q.q: What three-step phrase should you remember when you spot a hazard?
o: See it, Say it, Leave it
Find it, Fix it, Forget it
Stop it, Start it, Save it
Spot it, Stop it, Report it
q.why: When you spot a hazard, think Spot it, Stop it, Report it.

q.q: In the ICT room, who is 'the person in charge' you should report a danger to?
o: Your teacher
The pupil sitting next to you
Your form captain
The school caretaker only
q.why: In the ICT room the person in charge is your teacher.

q.q: According to the notes, most health and safety rules are what?
o: Hard to understand
Common sense
Only needed during exams
Only for adults at work
q.why: Most of the rules are common sense; we just need to behave sensibly.

q.q: Which of these is part of keeping 'our data' safe?
o: Keeping drinks away from the keyboard
Being careful who you share personal information with
Tidying cables away under the desk or in covers
Sitting with your back supported and feet flat
q.why: Your data is your own, so be careful where and with whom you share personal information.

q.q: A plug on a computer has a broken casing and loose wires. What is the main danger?
o: Backache
Data being lost
Electric shock
Eye strain
q.why: Damaged equipment such as loose wires and broken plugs can cause an electric shock.

q.q: What can happen if people do not stick to health and safety rules?
o: Better posture
Faster computers
Injury
Stronger passwords
q.why: Failing to stick to health and safety rules can result in injury.

q.q: What can cause backache when using a computer?
o: Sitting in the same position for a long time
Fitting blinds to the room's windows
Using a screen with an anti-glare coating
Resting your wrists on a wrist rest
q.why: Sitting too long in one position, or on a chair at the wrong height, causes backache.

q.q: Which item helps a pupil whose feet don't reach the floor?
o: A footrest
An anti-glare screen
A tilting monitor
A wrist rest
q.why: A footrest supports the legs and back when feet don't reach the floor.

q.q: Which describes good posture at a computer?
o: Sitting on the edge of the chair, twisted to one side
Leaning forward with the screen below your chin
Feet tucked under the chair and shoulders raised
Back supported, feet flat and screen at eye level
q.why: Good posture: back supported, feet flat, knees level with hips, shoulders relaxed, screen at eye level.

q.q: What serious problem could untreated backache lead to?
o: Nintendo thumb
Worsening eyesight
Damage to the spine
Eye strain
q.why: If backache isn't dealt with, it could cause damage to the spine.

q.q: Apart from sitting still too long, what else can cause backache?
o: Having the screen brightness too high
Having your chair at the wrong height
Looking at a screen near a window
Typing with your wrists bent
q.why: Backache can be caused by sitting in the same position for long periods or having your chair at the wrong height.

q.q: How does an adjustable chair help prevent backache?
o: It reminds you to take a break every hour
It keeps your wrists straight while typing
You can set the height and back support to fit your body
It stops glare from reaching the screen
q.why: An adjustable chair lets you set the height and back support to fit your body.

q.q: How do regular breaks help prevent backache?
o: They give your eyes a rest from the screen
Getting up and moving stops your muscles getting stiff
They stop your wrists repeating the same movement
They let the computer cool down
q.why: Getting up and moving stops your muscles getting stiff. Rest for eyes and wrists helps other problems.

q.q: How often do the notes suggest you stand up, stretch and move about?
o: Every 5 minutes
Once a day
Every 20–30 minutes
Every 2 hours
q.why: Every 20–30 minutes, stand up, stretch and move about for a minute.

q.q: Where should your screen be when you sit at a computer?
o: Above your head so you look up
Below your desk so you look down
At about eye level, straight in front of you
Off to one side so you turn your head
q.why: The screen should be at about eye level, straight in front of you.

q.q: Why does good posture help prevent backache?
o: It cuts down reflections on the screen
It makes the screen easier to read
It keeps your spine in its natural shape
It stops your fingers repeating movements
q.why: Good posture keeps your spine in its natural shape.

q.q: Rory spends three hours gaming hunched on the edge of his bed. The next day his back aches. What was the main cause?
o: He was sitting too far from the screen
His back was curved in the same position for a long time
The TV screen was too bright
He pressed the same buttons over and over
q.why: Sitting in the same curved position for a long time causes backache.

q.q: When sitting correctly, where should your knees be?
o: Roughly level with your hips
Pressed against the desk
Much higher than your hips
Tucked under the chair
q.why: Good posture has knees roughly level with your hips.

q.q: Which pair of solutions both help prevent backache?
o: A wrist rest and an anti-glare screen
An angled keyboard and blinds
Window blinds and a footrest
A footrest and not slouching
q.why: Footrests and good posture (no slouching) combat backache; wrist rests and anti-glare screens help with RSI and eye strain.

q.q: What causes eye strain?
o: Using a keyboard without a wrist rest
Typing with your wrists bent
Sitting on a chair at the wrong height
Looking at a screen continuously for a long time
q.why: Eye strain is caused by continuously looking at a screen for a long period of time.

q.q: What makes eye strain worse?
o: Typing slowly with straight wrists
Resting your wrists on a wrist rest
Putting your feet on a footrest
Reflection and glare from bright lights
q.why: Reflection and glare from bright lights, such as sunlight on the screen, make eye strain worse.

q.q: Which is NOT a symptom of eye strain?
o: Sore eyes
Worsening eyesight
Headaches
Numb thumbs
q.why: Numb thumbs are a sign of RSI, not eye strain.

q.q: Why should blinds be fitted to ICT room windows?
o: To keep the room warm in winter
To stop people looking in at the computers
To stop sunlight causing glare on screens
To stop the screens overheating
q.why: Blinds stop bright sunlight causing glare on the screen.

q.q: Where is the best place to position a monitor?
o: Away from direct sunlight
Facing a bright window
Very close to your face
Directly under a bright lamp
q.why: Position your monitor away from direct sunlight to reduce reflections.

q.q: What is an anti-glare screen?
o: A screen that makes text bigger automatically
A screen that switches off when you look away
A screen with a coating that cuts down reflections
A screen that can tilt and swivel
q.why: An anti-glare screen has a coating that cuts down reflections.

q.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
o: Every 20 seconds, look away from the screen for 20 minutes
Sit 20 cm from the screen for no more than 20 minutes
Take a 20-minute break after every 20 pages you read
Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
q.why: Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

q.q: In the 20-20-20 rule, 20 feet is about how far?
o: 60 metres
6 metres
20 metres
2 metres
q.why: 20 feet is about 6 metres.

q.q: How does a suitable screen size help prevent eye strain?
o: It uses less electricity so it is less bright
It stops sunlight from reaching the screen
It lets you sit closer to the screen
Text and images are big enough to read without squinting
q.why: A suitable screen size makes text and images big enough to read without squinting.

q.q: Aoife scrolls on her phone for hours in bed in a dark room. Which problem is she most at risk of?
o: Data loss
Backache from a wrong chair height
Eye strain
Electric shock
q.why: Phones count too: scrolling for hours in a dark room is a recipe for tired, sore eyes.

q.q: Sunlight from a window is reflecting off Ben's monitor. Which is the best fix?
o: Turn up the keyboard backlight
Move the monitor out of direct sunlight
Sit closer to the screen
Use a footrest
q.why: Positioning the monitor away from direct sunlight reduces reflections and glare.

q.q: Why do regular breaks help with eye strain?
o: They make the screen bigger
They stop sunlight shining on the screen
They give your eyes a rest from focusing on the screen
They keep your wrists straight
q.why: Breaks give your eyes a rest from focusing on the screen.

q.q: Which pair of solutions both help prevent eye strain?
o: A wrist rest and an angled keyboard
Window blinds and an anti-glare screen
A footrest and window blinds
A footrest and an adjustable chair
q.why: Blinds and anti-glare screens reduce glare; footrests and wrist rests help backache and RSI.

q.q: What does RSI stand for?
o: Repetitive Strain Injury
Regular Sitting Injury
Repetitive Stress Illness
Repeated Screen Injury
q.why: RSI = Repetitive Strain Injury.

q.q: What causes RSI?
o: Glare from bright lights
Sitting on a chair at the wrong height
Looking at a screen for a long time
Making the same movement again and again
q.why: RSI happens when you constantly make the same movement again and again.

q.q: Which body parts does RSI usually affect?
o: The bones in your lower back
The joints in your wrists and fingers
The muscles around your eyes
The joints in your knees and ankles
q.why: RSI usually affects the joints in your wrists and fingers.

q.q: Which item helps prevent RSI?
o: A footrest
A wrist rest
Window blinds
An anti-glare screen
q.why: A wrist rest supports your wrists so they stay straight.

q.q: What is 'Nintendo thumb'?
o: Sore or numb thumbs from gaming for a long time
Eye strain caused by a handheld console
A type of games controller with a thumbstick
Backache from holding a console too low
q.why: Nintendo thumb is a form of RSI from playing games for a long time.

q.q: In extreme cases, what can RSI lead to?
o: Headaches
Worsening eyesight
Damage to the spine
Arthritis
q.why: In extreme cases RSI can lead to arthritis (painful, swollen joints).

q.q: Which of these activities could lead to RSI?
o: Working in a hot, stuffy room
Texting for hours every day
Looking at a bright screen
Sitting with your back unsupported
q.why: Typing, texting, clicking a mouse and pressing controller buttons are repeated movements that can lead to RSI.

q.q: Why should you keep your wrists straight when typing?
o: Straight wrists make you type faster
Straight wrists stop backache
Bent wrists put extra strain on the joints
Bent wrists cause eye strain
q.why: Bent wrists put extra strain on the joints.

q.q: How does adjusting your keyboard to a comfortable angle help?
o: The keys become easier to see in sunlight
Your hands and wrists aren't bent awkwardly
Your back is kept in its natural shape
You can see the screen at eye level
q.why: A comfortable keyboard angle means your hands and wrists aren't bent awkwardly.

q.q: Conor plays the same game for six hours and his thumbs go numb. What is the best advice?
o: Use a footrest
Use an anti-glare screen
Sit closer to the TV
Take regular breaks to rest the joints
q.why: Breaks rest the muscles and joints from repeating the same movement; the other options help eye strain or backache.

q.q: Which is NOT a way to combat RSI?
o: Keeping wrists straight
Using an anti-glare screen
Using a wrist rest
Taking regular breaks
q.why: An anti-glare screen helps eye strain, not RSI.

q.q: What can RSI cause?
o: Headaches and sore eyes
Electric shocks and burns to the hands
Damage to the spine and lower back
Extreme pain and damage to the joints
q.why: RSI can cause extreme pain and damage to the joints.

q.q: A data entry worker types all day. Which health problem is she most likely to get from the typing itself?
o: Eye strain from glare
A trip injury
An electric shock
RSI
q.why: Typing all day is a repeated movement, which can lead to RSI.

q.q: What is ergonomics?
o: The science of making computers process data faster
The set of laws that protect employees at work
The study of how viruses spread between computers
The science of designing safe, comfortable hardware and furniture for humans
q.why: Ergonomics is designing equipment that fits the human body.

q.q: How many times did PlayStation officially change the design of its PS4 controller?
o: Twice
Once
Three times
Ten times
q.why: PlayStation officially changed the PS4 controller design three times.

q.q: How much did Microsoft say it spent designing its Xbox One controller?
o: Hundreds of millions
A few thousand
About one million
Hundreds of thousands
q.why: Microsoft spent 'hundreds of millions' designing its Xbox One controller.

q.q: Why do console companies spend so much on ergonomic controllers?
o: So the controllers last longer before breaking
So players need to take more breaks
So the controllers are cheaper to make
So you can play for longer with less chance of getting sore
q.why: A comfortable controller means you play for longer, which is good for the companies.

q.q: Which is an example of ergonomic equipment?
o: An adjustable chair
A web browser
A USB memory stick
Anti-virus software
q.why: An adjustable chair is designed to fit the user's body.

q.q: Which ergonomic equipment helps prevent RSI?
o: A tilt-and-swivel monitor on a stand
A footrest that supports your legs
An anti-glare screen filter
An ergonomic keyboard with split or angled keys
q.why: Split or angled keys keep wrists straight, which helps prevent RSI.

q.q: A tilt-and-swivel monitor mainly helps with which problems?
o: Eye strain, neck and back ache
Trips over trailing cables
Overheating of the computer
RSI in the wrists and fingers
q.why: A tilt-and-swivel monitor lets you adjust screen angle and height, helping eye strain and neck and back ache.

q.q: Even with a very comfortable ergonomic controller, what should you still do?
o: Keep your own safety in mind and take breaks
Play for as long as you like without stopping
Hold the controller tighter
Sit nearer the screen
q.why: It's very important to keep your own safety in mind however comfortable the equipment feels.

q.q: Which ergonomic feature does a shaped mouse have?
o: Its height and back rest can be changed
It cuts down reflections
It fits the shape of the hand
It supports feet that don't reach the floor
q.why: A shaped controller or mouse fits the shape of the hand, helping prevent RSI.

q.q: Which problem does an anti-glare screen filter help with?
o: Backache
Spine damage
RSI
Eye strain
q.why: An anti-glare filter cuts down reflections, helping eye strain.

q.q: Which of these everyday items do the notes say is designed using ergonomics?
o: The size of a computer's memory
The speed of a broadband connection
The colour of a website
The curve of a gaming chair
q.why: The shape of your phone, the angle of a laptop keyboard and the curve of a gaming chair are designed using ergonomics.

q.q: Why is a comfortable controller good for the company that makes it?
o: People keep using their products for longer
It costs less to make
It works on every brand of console
It never needs replacing
q.why: Comfortable products get used for longer, so people keep using their products.

q.q: Which piece of ergonomic equipment helps prevent backache?
o: An anti-glare filter
A footrest
A shaped mouse
A wrist rest
q.why: A footrest supports feet that don't reach the floor, helping prevent backache.

q.q: What is a hacker?
o: A program that copies itself between files
Someone employed to repair broken computers
An unauthorised person who breaks into a system
An employee who deletes a file by mistake
q.why: A hacker is an unauthorised person who breaks into a system and gains access to data by illegal means.

q.q: What is cyber security?
o: Keeping cables tidy in the ICT room
Protecting our bodies when using computers
Designing comfortable computer equipment
Protecting our data from being damaged
q.why: Protecting our data from being damaged is called cyber security.

q.q: An employee accidentally emails a customer list to the wrong person. What type of threat is this?
o: A virus
A careless insider threat
A system crash
A hacker
q.why: It comes from inside the organisation, though it was not deliberate, so it is a careless insider threat.

q.q: What is the best way to recover work after a computer is damaged?
o: Change your password
Run anti-virus software
Restore it from a backup
Buy a new monitor
q.why: Regular backups on another device or in the cloud let work be restored.

q.q: Which of these is a threat to data?
o: A wrist rest
A footrest
A system crash
Window blinds
q.why: A crash affecting the hard drive may damage key sections of data.

q.q: What is an insider threat?
o: Damage caused by a crash inside the hard drive
A threat that comes from someone inside the organisation
A hacker who breaks in from outside the company
A virus hidden inside an email attachment
q.why: An insider threat comes from someone inside an organisation, and can be deliberate or careless.

q.q: A former employee who was sacked deletes important files on purpose. What threat is this?
o: A deliberate (malicious) insider threat
A system crash
A careless insider threat
An accidental loss of data
q.why: Data sabotaged by former employees committing malicious acts is an insider threat.

q.q: What name is sometimes given to careless insiders?
o: Spiders or crawlers
Recipients
Pawns or goofs
Hackers
q.why: Careless insiders are sometimes called pawns or goofs.

q.q: What is the best protection against nearly every data problem?
o: A backup kept somewhere else
Up-to-date anti-virus software
Meaningful file names
A long, strong password
q.why: The best protection against nearly every data problem is a backup: a second copy kept somewhere else.

q.q: Which is a suitable place to keep a backup of your school work?
o: A second folder on the same computer
Your school network area or Google Drive
The same USB stick as the original
The Recycle Bin
q.why: Keep backups on another device or in the cloud, such as your school network area or Google Drive.

q.q: A file on your computer has a virus. What should you do?
o: Move the file into a different folder on the same computer so it is kept apart
Scan and remove it with up-to-date anti-virus software, then restore a clean copy
Email the file to your teacher and ask them to check it on their computer
Rename the file and change its extension so the virus cannot find or open it
q.why: Use up-to-date anti-virus software to scan and remove it, and restore a clean copy from a backup.

q.q: You can't remember the name of a file you saved last week. What is a good way to find it?
o: Restore an old backup over all your work
Search by date modified or by a word in the file
Run anti-virus software on the folder
Ask the network technician to reset your password
q.why: Search by date modified or by a word in the file, or sort the folder by date.

q.q: What should you do if you forget your school password?
o: Use the password reset or ask the technician or teacher, then set a new strong one
Keep guessing different passwords until the computer finally lets you back in
Write your new password on a sticky note on the screen
Log in using a friend's account until you remember your own password again
q.why: Use the forgotten-password reset (or ask the technician/teacher), set a new strong password and never write it where others can see.

q.q: Saved files keep going missing because you can't find them. Which solution do the notes suggest?
o: Install more anti-virus software
Save every file to the desktop
Make the files larger so they stand out
Organise work in sensible folders with meaningful file names
q.why: Organise work in sensible folders with meaningful names, and use the search tool.

q.q: Why do hackers often use viruses?
o: Viruses make computers faster to break into
Viruses can attack and seriously damage files
Viruses delete the hacker's tracks automatically
Viruses give the hacker a new password
q.why: Hackers often use viruses, which can attack and seriously damage files.

q.q: An office worker leaves a work laptop on a bus. What type of threat is this?
o: A hacker
A virus
A system crash
A careless insider threat
q.why: Leaving a laptop on a bus is careless behaviour by someone inside the organisation.

q.q: Which threat to data is described as data being lost or deleted by mistake?
o: Insider threats
Accidents
System crashes
Hackers
q.why: Accidents: data can be lost accidentally or deleted by mistake.

q.q: When was the Health and Safety at Work Act introduced?
q.why: The Act was introduced in 1974; 1978 is the NI Order and 1992 the Display Screen Equipment Regulations.

q.q: What does 'duty of care' mean for an employer?
o: They must give employees a day off each week
They must check employees' emails every day
They are legally responsible for keeping employees safe
They must teach employees how to use every program
q.why: A duty of care means employers are legally responsible for keeping employees safe.

q.q: Which employer regulation helps prevent eye strain?
o: Providing adjustable chairs
Providing anti-glare screen filters
Providing wrist rests
Providing foot supports
q.why: Anti-glare filters reduce eye strain.

q.q: Who does the Health and Safety at Work Act set duties for?
o: Employees only, not their employers
Schools, teachers and pupils only
Employers, employees and some self-employed people
Employers only, not their employees
q.why: The Act sets duties for employers, employees and certain self-employed people.

q.q: In Northern Ireland, which law gives the same duties as the 1974 Act?
o: The Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978
The Display Screen Equipment Regulations 1974
The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Health and Safety at Work (NI) Act 1992
q.why: In NI the same duties come from the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978.

q.q: Which regulations contain the detailed rules for computer users?
o: The school's ICT Acceptable Use Policy
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
The Health and Safety at Work (NI) Order 1978
The Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992
q.why: The detailed rules for computer users are the Display Screen Equipment Regulations 1992.

q.q: Which employer regulation helps prevent backache?
o: Providing adjustable chairs
Providing anti-glare filters
Providing window blinds
Paying for eye tests
q.why: Adjustable chairs help prevent backache.

q.q: For which employees must an employer pay for eye tests?
o: Regular screen users
Only employees who already wear glasses
Only employees over 40
Every employee, whether they use a screen or not
q.why: Employers must pay for eye tests for regular screen users, and glasses if needed for screen work.

q.q: Planning work so employees get regular breaks or changes of activity helps protect against which problems?
o: Glare and electric shocks
Only eye strain
Eye strain, RSI and backache
Only RSI
q.why: Regular breaks help with eye strain, RSI and backache.

q.q: What should an employer carry out to check each employee's desk set-up is safe?
o: A system backup
A password reset
A virus scan
A workstation assessment
q.why: Employers carry out workstation assessments and give training on safe use.

q.q: Providing suitable lighting and window blinds protects employees against what?
o: Damage to the spine
Glare and eye strain
Backache
RSI in the wrists
q.why: Suitable lighting and blinds protect against glare and eye strain.

q.q: An employee complains her feet don't touch the floor at her desk. What must her employer provide?
o: An anti-glare filter
A tiltable screen
A foot support (footrest)
An eye test
q.why: Employers must provide foot supports for those who need them.

q.q: What is an employee?
o: A person who works for an employer
A person who repairs computers
A person who owns a company
A self-employed person who works alone
q.why: An employee works for an employer, who has a duty of care to them.

q.q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight things employers must do for ICT users?
o: Provide tiltable screens
Provide a laptop for each employee to use at home
Pay for eye tests for regular screen users
Give training on safe use
q.why: The eight regulations cover screens, filters, chairs, footrests, breaks, eye tests, lighting and assessments/training.

q.q: Which two employer regulations both help prevent backache?
o: Providing eye tests and suitable lighting
Providing anti-glare filters and blinds
Providing anti-glare filters and eye tests
Providing adjustable chairs and foot supports
q.why: Adjustable chairs and footrests both protect against backache.

q.q: Why is the 1974 Act important for workplaces where people use IT?
o: It protects employees and the public from work activities, including IT
It stops hackers breaking into office networks
It says that only trained adults may use a computer
It decides how much employees should be paid
q.why: The Act protects employees and the public from work activities, including those that involve IT.
